cards.0655: A man in his early forties takes the brush out of the bag in the footwell of his van on a Tuesday because he is on a stranger's gate with the same lump of old gloss on the back of the frame, and he does the exact job he promised a woman of seventy-eight in about ten minutes, and it is easy, and it is the easiest thing he has done in a fortnight. He has proved his own sentence out loud and he cannot say a word about it. He cannot go back up that road and admit it was ten minutes, because saying it was ten minutes means saying he knew, and he did know, and the only reason he said nothing in that kitchen was so that a woman would not have to be thanked. He puts the brush in his back pocket at half past twelve because he is going up a ladder and cannot carry the bag, and he does not think about it again until 0658.
cards.0656: A woman in her late forties buys a wire brush out of a bucket in a shop on the ring road on a Monday morning because she has a chisel and no brush and the drops on the back of that gate frame are one solid lump under old gloss, and she will not ring him and ask for one, because he will say yes, and because she has known since the sixteenth of July what she would do with a yes. She spends the whole of that Monday on a house she is clearing on the far side of the ring road with the new brush, which is a bad brush, on work that has nothing to do with any gate, and she does not knock at number twelve, and the reason she does not knock is not that the door would not open.
cards.0657: A woman in her early thirties from number ten, who taped a back room window in May and was told no in three seconds about a gate and did not ask why, walks up three doors on a Thursday afternoon and knocks, and the door opens in about a second, because the woman at number twelve cannot say no to somebody who has knocked. She does not go in. She stands on the step for about a minute and says one sentence, which is about the tape, and the woman at number twelve does not ask her in, and she goes back down the road. She is the only person on that road who has a standing to knock and has never used it, and the reason she has never used it is that she was let in once when she was nineteen and stayed too long.
cards.0658: The man in his early forties works out, in a unit, that the brush is in the back pocket of a jacket on a hook and not in the bag, and that it has been in the back pocket of a jacket on a hook since the twentieth of July, and he does not know how it got there because a thing cannot get into a pocket. He has decided to do the gate. He goes to a shop on the ring road and buys a brush with his own money and it is not his brush. He puts it in the van and he does not book a Wednesday, and the brush is in the van for a fortnight and never touches a gate, and a man buying a tool for a job he is not going to do is what a woman buying a tool for a job she cannot start did on the twenty-sixth of July, and neither of them knows the other has.
cards.0659: The woman in her late forties knocks on a Saturday morning and is let in in about a second, and gets the chisel and her own brush and goes out to the back of the gate and cuts the drop bolts out, one solid lump of old gloss over two of them, and it takes four hours and not ten minutes and her hands are cut inside the palm twice. The woman at number twelve watches from the kitchen window and does not come out and cannot say thank you properly and the woman who has come is not able to let her. At about half past three she comes in through the front door to wash her hands at the kitchen sink, which is at the back of the house past the front room, and she puts the brush down on the sideboard in the front room because it is in her hand and the sideboard is the first flat thing, and the sideboard has nothing else on it. She goes. The gate lifts and swings and does not come in on the path for the first time since it was put on and nobody is standing at it.
cards.0660: The woman in her late seventies has a wire brush on a sideboard in her front room and has had it since the Saturday. She cannot ask what it is for. She cannot put it in the bin because she does not know what a thing is before you bin it. She cannot carry it into the passage because it would be in everybody's way and it would be a thing she could be asked about, and she cannot be asked about things. She tries it on the kitchen windowsill over the sink and that is worse, because she looks at it while she is at the sink. And she puts it back on the sideboard, and the sideboard is where it lives, and from that day she does not sit in the front room, which is the only room in that house anybody has ever sat in.
cards.0661: The woman in her late forties has cuts inside both palms and does not go to anybody about them and cannot ask anybody about anything. She has four hours of gate work in her arms and no invoice and no money for it and a thing already delivered that nobody has thanked her for and cannot. And she has a wire brush in her own van that she bought for a job that is now finished, and a job that is finished is a job a tool has nothing to be for, and she puts it in the drawer under the bench in the van and shuts it, and the shut is the whole of the chapter.
cards.0662: The woman in her late fifties at number nine, in from lates at ten past midnight, is told by her sister in the middle of something else, without being asked, that somebody has been at the gate at number twelve. She works out, standing at her own sink, that the man who gave her the stool on the twenty-seventh of May is the man who has been in that passage, because her sister said a woman has had a light put in and a woman cannot do that. She now knows where the stool came from and she cannot say thank you to a woman of seventy-eight who cannot be thanked and cannot ask the woman a single question about where it came from. She moves the stool out of her kitchen and puts it in her front room, because the kitchen is where you eat and the front room is where you put a thing you do not know what to do with.
cards.0663: The woman in her late seventies goes up the stairs of her own house at about ten at night on a Friday, alone, with a torch, for the first time since the spring, and there are two rooms on the top floor with the doors open and a landing nobody walks on, and she has never seen the landing in the dark. There is a fixed ladder to a hatch over the landing, and there is a high level cistern on the roof space with a ballcock on it she has never seen, and the ballcock is leaking, and it has been leaking long enough to put a soft place in the plaster and a stain down the wall behind the bathroom, and if it goes on four more weeks it comes through the ceiling of the room she does not sit in. She puts her thumb in the plaster about the width of a thumb and then she goes back down the stairs and puts the cloth back in the bowl under the tap and the tap goes on dripping, and she has not asked anybody for anything and nothing has been done.
cards.0664: The woman in her late seventies decides on a Wednesday morning that the front room is now a room with a thing in it she cannot identify, and that she will not sit in a room like that, and that the only place a thing can live where nobody can explain it is where everybody walks. She puts the wire brush on the floor of her own passage at about half past ten in the morning, in the middle, where somebody will have to step over it or ask her about it. Then she goes out of the front door and round the side of the house and lifts the latch of her own gate and stands it open and does not go out into the road and does not shut it, and goes back in and shuts the front door behind her. There is no one in the road. The gate has not been open since before Christmas and nothing about it is solved, and the first thing anybody does about a gate that has been standing open for a week is not in this batch.
